claims.text: High configurational entropy promotes preferential surface segregation of Al and Cr during high-temperature exposure.
Al and Cr are thermodynamically stable oxide-forming elements in Fe–Cr–Al high-entropy alloys.
Surface segregation of Al and Cr causes nucleation and growth of a continuous, dense, and adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale.
A continuous, dense, and adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale provides oxidation resistance.
Minor Y additions stabilize the protective oxide scale by mitigating spallation.
Lower concentrations of Al and Cr lead to discontinuous or porous, less-protective oxide layers.
High configurational entropy retards diffusion of nonprotective oxide-forming species.
High configurational entropy retards coarsening of nonprotective oxides.
Retarded diffusion and coarsening favor chemically driven segregation of Al and Cr to the surface.
Surface-segregated Al and Cr nucleate a protective oxide scale.
The interplay of composition, segregation kinetics, and scale stability governs oxidation resistance.
Increasing Al and Cr concentrations will produce a more uniform and adherent protective oxide scale than the lower-Al/Cr baseline.
Increasing Al and Cr concentrations will reduce oxide-thickness growth rates relative to the baseline.
Minor Y additions will reduce scale spallation relative to alloys without Y.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to Fe–Cr–Al-based high-entropy alloys oxidized at 900–1100 °C.
Samples will be oxidized in air or controlled oxygen partial pressures for 100–500 hours at 900–1100 °C.
Alloys with systematically varied Al, Cr, and trace Y contents will be compared under identical oxidation conditions.
A lack of correlation between increased oxide-former content, surface segregation, and formation of a continuous adherent scale would falsify the hypothesis.
